title: Proposal: a concise syntax offering a more general, less brittle alternative to Markdown and its variants
body:
The popularity of [Markdown](https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/syntax) and its innumerable variants shows clear and widespread demand for markup syntax that is more concise, and easier to type and read, than the venerable SGML-style syntax that still underlies HTML, XML, and XHTML. But Markdown-style languages, while perhaps visually appealing, bring important limitations and brittleness: each flavor directly supports only a small subset of the rich functionality of HTML, is [hard to specify precisely or standardize](https://commonmark.org), and is hard to extend with richer markup features without creating a further exponential explosion of syntactic conflicts and subtleties. HTML is already an "abstract syntax" with two concrete syntaxes (HTML and XML) plus an "in-memory syntax" (the DOM). Should HTML evolve further to offer a third concrete syntax, which would be more concise to type and read directly (akin to Markdown), while retaining the full power, expressiveness, and extensibility of HTML (unlike Markdown)? I'd like to call for thoughts and discussion on this question in general, while also proposing one possible template for what such a more concise but general concrete syntax could look like: [MinML](https://bford.info/2022/12/28/minml/). In brief, MinML provides a more concise substitute for the traditional SGML-derived "meta-syntax" without constraining or otherwise affecting the element-level syntax of HTML. That is, MinML syntax makes HTML a bit more concise and arguably easier to type and read, while supporting all the same elements and markup expressiveness as HTML, both now and in the future. As a few quick illustrative examples, one writes _emphasis_ as `em[emphasis]` in MinML rather than `emphasis`. Headings look like `h1[section title]` rather than `

section title

`. Links look like `a{href=http://bford.info/}[my home page]`. Character references look like `[star]` rather than `☆`. Quoted strings like "quote" look like `"[quote]` rather than `“quote”`. Comments look like `-[comment]` instead of ``. For more details, please see [my blog post introducing MinML](https://bford.info/2022/12/28/minml/). MinML intentionally stops short of being quite as "visual" as Markdown syntax, while being more concise than SGML syntax (in particular by replacing end tags with end brackets), all while preserving compatibility with HTML's full abstract syntax. The intent is that anything written HTML (or XHTML) can be automatically converted to MinML, or vice versa, so the concise meta-syntax should never entail a loss of expressiveness like Markdown does. I see no urgent need for MinML to replace HTML as an "on-the-wire" syntax transmitted over HTTP connections. Rather, I see such a concise HTML syntax as something that website builders like Wordpress, Hugo, etc., as well as interactive text-entry systems (like GitHub issues) might support in addition to (or instead of) Markdown. There is already [an experimental Hugo extension to support MinML syntax](https://github.com/bford/hugo). Of course this is still at an early stage, and it remains to be seen whether MinML or something like it can prove "concise enough" or "attractive enough" in people's perceptions to make it a practical alternative to Markdown-style syntax. But at least starting this discussion is the main purpose of this post. All feedback is welcome.
